lessons.title: Pointers to Functions
intro: A function sits somewhere in memory too, so it has an address. int (*f)(int); declares f as a pointer to a function that takes an int and returns an int. The brackets around *f matter: without them, it would be a function that returns an int *.
A function's name without () is its address: f = twice;. Call through the pointer like a normal function: f(5), or the old style (*f)(5).
The point: you can hand a function to another function. The example prints a table for any function you give it.

code: int square(int x) { return x * x; }

options: A pointer to a function that takes an int and returns an int
A function that returns a pointer
exercises.explanation: Read it from the name outwards: f is a pointer (*), to a function taking (int), returning int.

code: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
int sub(int a, int b) { return a - b; }
exercises.explanation: op points to sub, so op(10, 4) is sub(10, 4).
The name without brackets is the function's address. With brackets, you'd call it.

exercises.prompt: This program doesn't compile. Which line is wrong?
code: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
exercises.explanation: Without brackets, int *op(int, int) declares a function returning int *. It must be int (*op)(int, int).

exercises.prompt: Why hand a function to another function?
options: So the same code can do different jobs, like sorting by different rules
exercises.explanation: table() doesn't need to know what f calculates. The next lesson uses this for sorting.

code: int square(int x) { return x * x; }
exercises.explanation: apply calls f twice: square(square(3)) = square(9) = 81.

lessons.title: qsort
intro: stdlib.h has a sort that works for any array: qsort(array, count, size of one element, compare). It doesn't know what's in your array, so you give it a compare function.

The compare function gets two const void * pointers to two elements. It returns a negative number if the first should come first, 0 if they're equal, and a positive number if the second should come first. Inside, you turn the void pointers into the real type.
To sort the other way round, swap the two. To sort structs, compare one field, like the score or the name with strcmp.

code: struct player { char name[8]; int score; };

exercises.prompt: What must a compare function for qsort return when a should come before b?
exercises.explanation: Negative: a first. Zero: equal. Positive: b first.

exercises.prompt: Sort ints from small to big.
exercises.explanation: a - b is negative when a is smaller, so a comes first. (< would only give 0 or 1.)
The compare function returns b - a, so bigger numbers come first.

exercises.prompt: Why does the compare function get const void * pointers?
options: qsort sorts any type, so it can't know the real one
exercises.explanation: void * means "a pointer to something". You know what it really is, so you turn it into that.

exercises.prompt: This program stops with an error. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explanation: The third argument is the size of one element: sizeof(int), or sizeof v[0], which can't go wrong.

exercises.prompt: qsort(names, n, sizeof names[0], by_name); by_name compares with strcmp. In what order are the names?
exercises.explanation: strcmp is negative when the first name comes first in the alphabet.

lessons.title: Tables of Functions
intro: An array of function pointers turns a choice into a lookup: instead of a long if-else chain, you find the right entry in a table and call it. Menus, calculators and even the Unix kernel's system calls work like this.
A typedef makes these types readable: typedef int (*Op)(int, int); and then Op ops[4];.
Put a name and a function together in a struct, and you get a command table: to add a command, you add one line to the table.

code: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
int sub(int a, int b) { return a - b; }
int mul(int a, int b) { return a * b; }
int divide(int a, int b) { return a / b; }
int calc(char *name, int a, int b) {

exercises.prompt: typedef int (*Op)(int, int); What is Op?
options: A name for the type "pointer to a function taking two ints and returning an int"
exercises.explanation: After the typedef, Op f; declares a function pointer.

code: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
int mul(int a, int b) { return a * b; }

exercises.explanation: run is the function pointer in the struct.

exercises.prompt: Why use a table instead of a long if-else chain?
options: A new command is just one new line in the table
exercises.explanation: The code that searches and calls never changes.

exercises.prompt: In ops[i](a, b), what happens first?
options: ops[i] picks a function pointer, then it's called with a and b
exercises.explanation: The [i] comes first, then the call.
First the type, then the table that uses it, then a call through the table.
